newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Chirac backs Czech EU membership in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Chirac backs Czech EU membership in 2000.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, underlining French backing for the rapid integration of Eastern Europe with the West, pledged his support for Czech membership of the European Union in 2000 and of NATO a year earlier.
Chirac, speaking after talks with Czech President Vaclav Havel, also reiterated his belief that Romania should be among the first group of countries to be invited to join NATO.

"I was able to confirm to the president that France unreservedly supports both the candidacy of the Czech Republic for the European Union, of which I think and hope it will be a member in the year 2000, and of NATO," he told reporters.
The Czech Republic, along with Poland and Hungary, are the leading candidates to become the next new members of both the EU and North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

Chirac, on the first fay of a two-day state visit, said France wanted a NATO summit in Madrid to approve a declaration on the candidacy of the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary "so that they can truly be integrated in 1999".
"We want, moreover, that Romania be part of this first group and I know that the Czech Republic has no objections to this," Chirac said.

The French leader has made similar statements of support for Polish and Hungarian membership in 2000 and backed Romania's inclusion in the first wave of NATO enlargement during a recent visit to Bucharest.
Chirac's tour of East European capitals, which began in Warsaw last September, has largely been aimed at erasing the belief that France was hostile to their integration with Western organisations.
Chirac's predecessor, the late Francois Mitterrand, said in Prague in 1990 that it would be decades before the first post-Communist central European states joined the EU.
But Czech officials have expressed concern at Chirac's insistence that NATO reach a new security relationship with Russia before inviting new members to join.
Czech leaders have said there can be no turning back on NATO enlargement and have warned the big powers against struggling for influence in Central Europe.
French officials have said the Czechs seem more interested in the EU's single market than in France's vision of the EU as an integrated social and defence alliance.
But Chirac said he and Havel felt the same about building a European economic, political and security system.

Havel, in an interview shown on Czech television on Tuesday, urged his countrymen not to be apathetic about NATO membership. Opinion polls show only about a third of Czechs support membership -- far fewer than in Poland or Hungary.
Havel said in an interview with French daily Le Monde this week that he hoped to hear exactly when EU accession talks would begin.

"President Chirac has assured me of his firm conviction that the Amsterdam summit will put an end to the EU intergovernmnetal conference and that they will keep to the planned schedule," he told reporters.
